en: The Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables, translated by the Yuezhi Śramaṇa Lokakṣema during the Later Han Dynasty.
(1) Once there was a bhikṣu who was intelligent and wise; at one time he fell gravely ill, and his disciple asked him:
"Have you attained arhatship?
He replied, "I have not yet attained it."
"He has not yet attained the stage of Non-returning.
[The monk] asked, "Your Reverence’s Way is lofty and your fame is far-reaching; why have you not yet reached it?"
The preceptor replied,
"He has already attained the fruit of the Once-returner, but the two higher fruits have not yet been realized.
He then questioned him:
"Having already attained the stage of 'Once-returner' (Sakṛdāgāmin), what obstacle prevents one from reaching the state of a True Person (Arhat)?

He replied: "I wish to behold Maitreya Buddha. At that time, during his three assemblies, twenty-eight billion people will attain the state of a True Person, and the number of Bodhisattvas will be beyond measure. The Tathāgata Maitreya’s majestic body shall be most sublime, measuring sixteen hundred *zhang* in height. The inhabitants of that land will all have the color of peach blossoms; their lifespan shall be eighty-four thousand years. The terrain will be level and upright, and food and clothing will appear spontaneously. The land of Jambudvīpa will be thirty thousand *li* in both width and length."
I wish to see these two, yet I do not take them to be true sages.
During the time of Maitreya Buddha, there will be two chief disciples: one named Miśraka-dāyaka and the other named Abhīkṣṇa-dāyaka. I wish to see them again and know how they compare to me.
The disciple asked again:
"From whom did you hear this?
The Upādhyāya replied:
"I have heard this from the Buddha’s sutras. The disciple said,
"In the midst of the toil and suffering of birth and death, if Maitreya possesses some extraordinary dharma, should we go to wait for him?"
He replied: "There is no difference.
How could there be any difference between the six perfections, the four immeasurables, the four ways of attracting beings, and the four noble truths? He replied:
"No. Even if one were equal to the other such that there was no difference between them, why wait?
Now that I have received the Buddha's grace, I shall instead go to Maitreya; I may likewise receive deliverance there without needing to wait for him."
The Upādhyāya said:
"Stop! You may depart for now; I shall reflect upon this."
Before the disciple had even gone out and reached the threshold of the door, he had already become a Perfected One (Zhēnrén).
The disciple returned and asked,
"What has happened?"
The Master said,
"He has already become a True Man.
The disciple bowed in reverence and said:
"In the mere instant of a stern rebuke, he has already attained the fruit of realization.

(2) Once, when a certain bhikṣu had attained meditative concentration, a wild fire could not burn him. People who saw him thought he was a ghost and struck him with axes, but their blades broke and would not penetrate his body.
Because his mind was single-minded, he did not enter [the fire]; because it was supple, he was not burned.

There was a man who had attained meditative concentration; when his disciples called him for a meal, he was unaware of them. Consequently, they went forward and pulled his arm, which extended to a length of over ten feet.
The disciple was afraid and immediately tied it up; fearing that once tied it could not be untied again, he intended to undo it.
When the master awoke from his meditation, he suffered from pain in his arm and questioned the disciple, who reported the matter exactly as it had happened.
The Master said:
"You did not understand my awakening and broke my arm.
When a person attains the state of meditative concentration, they become as supple as cotton; it is the same while in the mother's womb."
(3) Once, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was a bodhisattva who, upon being born and falling to the ground, caused the earth to tremble greatly, so that his parents were both terrified.
At that time, a true person (ṛṣi) lowered his head in prostration and offered a flower canopy as an offering.

Later, Chang left the household life; he was brilliant, wise, and possessed of eloquence. Although he was often dissolute and lacked formal discipline, those who heard what he said would immediately attain the Way.
At that time, there were two men who had both become bhikṣus; they had maintained pure precepts in a vihāra for many years, yet their minds remained unenlightened.
A celestial deity said to them,
"In that country there is a bhikṣu who has brought many to spiritual transformation and deliverance.
The two men immediately set out for that distant land to invite him back.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in that country who had been having an affair with a courtesan. The two of them sought an audience with him; one entered first, paid his respects, and sat to one side. The courtesan remained lying down as before, appearing exceedingly beautiful beyond compare in the world, yet she listened to the sutra with single-minded focus, free from any other thoughts, and thereby attained the stage of Stream-entry (srotāpatti). She prostrated herself and returned.
He further sent another man forward to pay his respects, question him, and sit and listen; seeing the woman lying there in a state of sexual dalliance, the man thought to himself:
"This man is defiled, dishonorable, and wicked; he has come from afar in vain suffering."
He then abandoned her and went outside.
The bhikṣu asked, "Why are you so distressed? Do you know that such views are heterodox?"
He said: "It has caused us to wander through the wilderness in hardship; following such a corrupt teacher as this leads to such dissolute conduct. He said:
"You have committed a great error.
The law for a scholar is simply to rectify the mind and listen with wisdom and understanding; why do you criticize right and wrong, give rise to evil thoughts, and cause others to gain nothing?"
They further straightened their hearts and entered together to listen to the sutras, whereupon they again attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
One of them attained Arhatship (arhat), while the teacher provided him with a guest-house and returned to his own country.
Later, the teacher took charge of the monastery and made extensive use of the monastic property; he indulged in lewdness and excessive pleasure.
When the assembly of monks deliberated on expelling him, a realized person said:
"Do not cast him out! Although he uses the property of the Sangha, he is able to bring many to transformation and deliverance."
He then stopped and did not pursue him.
His relatives went to him and said,
"Your former disciple may go to beg for you, providing all the necessary materials and provisions."
He immediately went to that country, obtained a great quantity of various treasures, and returned to repay the Sangha with double the amount.

(4) Long ago, there was a worthy man who served the Dharma with diligent effort; he fell ill and suddenly passed away. His wife and children wailed in grief and attachment, finding no solace in life. After his body had been cremated and the bones collected and buried, they neglected the sutras and the Way, and ceased offering incense and lamps. Although their family wealth was abundant, on the first and fifteenth days of the month, they would slaughter animals to prepare feasts, gather at his grave for assemblies, and weep until they were broken by their sorrow and lamentation.

The deceased, having perfected his virtue through the precepts, ascended to heaven; there, with his divine eye, he saw [the child] from afar and took pity on him, laughing at the height of his folly as he had been born as a young boy tending cattle nearby.

The ox died suddenly, and the boy began to wail and weep. He placed cut grass before it and tried to coax it to eat, but the ox merely bellowed and got up; they wept together face-to-face in this manner until the end of the day.
The crowd marveled and laughed, going together to rebuke him and ask:
"Whose son are you? When the ox dies, you should return and speak to your family; what benefit is there in wailing and weeping?"
"Did the cow know it was dying?
He replied, "I am not foolish."
"If the ox were still dead, there might yet be hope;
but your father died long ago—though you prepare a hundred kinds of food and wail together toward his remains, how can scorched bones know anything?
Upon hearing this, the assembly was suddenly enlightened.
He said, "I am originally your father; having been born in heaven through the grace of the Buddha, I have come to release you.
Thereupon, he returned to his celestial form and said, "If you wish to become like me, you must further increase your offerings to the Way."
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished.

His wife and children, both inside and outside the household, returned to their duties; through diligence, moral virtue, and the charity of providing relief, they were no longer troubled by grief, and all attained the fruit of the Path and were reborn in heaven simultaneously.
(5) In the midst of the ocean there was a country named Sihakṣetra, which produced many precious gems but lacked rock honey (*śarkarā*).

At that time, there was a merchant who brought more than five hundred wagons of rock honey and thought to himself: "If I present this to the king, the reward I receive will surely exceed what I would gain from selling it in the market. He then placed the rock honey at the gate of the royal palace and announced his purpose.
Thus, for many days and months, there was no one to question him. He spoke with resentment, saying:
"That king is also a human being, and I too am a human being; our eyes, ears, nose, mouths, and four great elements are all the same, yet I cannot even obtain a single audience or a word with him."
Why is this? Because the King’s merit and virtue surpass those of men.
I, too, shall perform meritorious deeds so that the King will unknowingly come to seek refuge with me.

Thereupon, he went forth to become a śramaṇa and made offerings of honey to the Triple Gem. Seeking a secluded place, he contemplated suffering, emptiness, and non-self; before even half the time had passed, his mind was liberated from all fetters and he attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). When those capable of attaining arhatship without moving from their spot cause the earth to tremble, Śakra and the various devas ought to come to offer consolation. Thus, the Lord of Devas and all the heavenly beings descended, paid homage, and rejoiced with him.
The bhikṣu asked the Lord of Devas, "What do you all do in the heavens? They replied:

"In the heavens there are four pleasure gardens for viewing; three of these are places of the five desires, while one is a place of the Way and its virtue. Within it, they may discuss the noble scriptures of the Buddha, or at times discuss those among the four classes of people in the world who are diligent in upholding the Dharma."
The bhikṣu asked:
"Regarding those who uphold the discourse, are they all of one kind, or are there degrees of depth?
The Lord of Devas replied:
"In general, when discussing virtuous persons, there have been three since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa for whom the devas have upheld the treatises without ever abandoning them.
The bhikṣu asked, "Who are these people?"
"Devānām-indra, explain this to me one by one.
Devānām-indra replied:
"In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a man who became a śramaṇa and made this vow to himself:"
"I shall practice walking meditation and roam about; I will not lie down to rest until I have attained the state of an Arhat.
Thereupon, he practiced walking meditation day and night until his feet were so worn that they bled, and a hundred birds followed him to peck at them. After three years, he attained the Way;
the devas praised and examined him, and there was none who did not pay him homage.
There was another man in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who also became a śramaṇa; he spread grass to make a mat and sat upon it, vowing to himself:
"I shall not rise until I have attained the Way."

However, when Āṭavika came, he only wished to sleep. [The Buddha] had a person make an awl eight inches long; whenever sleepiness came, it would prick both his thighs. Because of the pain from the sores, he did not sleep, and within one year, he attained the state of an Arhat.
The devas also marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
Furthermore, there was another person who had also become a śramaṇa in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; he dwelt in a mountain stone cave so steep and perilous that no one could ever go to or come from it.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, seeing his diligent practice, transformed himself into a water buffalo and stood before the bhikṣu, snorting and bellowing with its horns pointed at him, intending to gore him. The bhikṣu was greatly terrified and thought to himself:
"This place is inaccessible even to cattle; why is there such a creature here?"
"Could this not be the work of Māra?
He then cried out:
"Is this the doing of you, wicked Māra!"
The Māra, thinking he had been discovered, resumed his original form.
The bhikṣu said to the Māra:
"What do you fear that you seek from me?"
The Māra said:
"I saw that this practitioner was diligent and feared he would depart from my realm; therefore, I have come to terrify him.
The bhikṣu replied:

"The reason I have become a śramaṇa is that I seek deliverance from the world; I merely wish to see the Buddha with his marks and signs. Since the Buddha has departed from the world, none are able to see him. I have heard that Māra can transform himself into the body of a Buddha; if he manifests this for me, I shall no longer apply myself with diligence."

The Māra, thinking this must indeed be so, immediately transformed himself into a Buddha and stood before him. As he contemplated, he attained arhatship; the devas in the sky all proclaimed his boundless excellence, and the Māra’s remorse and poisonous anguish were instantly extinguished.
The Lord of Devas said to the bhikṣu:
"These three persons are praised by all the devas, and even now they do not cease.
The bhikṣu said to the Lord of Devas:
"These three men clearly understood suffering and emptiness, which is why they decayed their bodies.
Originally, I had no intention of being slighted by others; thus I practiced the quest for the Way and escaped the three realms. This too is marvelous, and I have attained Arhatship."
The devas replied, "Now he shall return to the heavens as the foremost among practitioners.
Thereupon, the devas paid their respects and departed.

Thereupon, when the king heard that the Master of Stone Honey had attained the Way through diligent practice, he went at once to prostrate himself and bow his head in apology for his past transgressions. He was subsequently appointed as State Preceptor; he caused the Triple Gem to flourish and brought peace to the nation, such that the blessings obtained and those delivered were beyond calculation.
6. Once there was a sick man whom various physicians could not cure. He went directly to seek refuge with the king, whose name was Sāhvata, and surrendered himself to the Great King, saying:
"I pray that you, out of compassion, will treat my illness."
The king immediately entrusted him to various physicians and commanded them to treat his illness.
The physicians informed the king:
"This medicine cannot be obtained."
The king asked the physicians, "What is the name of that medicine?
They replied, "There are no five-poisoned people in the world whose flesh can be used to make a broth; by taking this, one will be cured."
What are the five poisons? First, the absence of a mind of lustful desire;

second, the absence of a mind of anger and resentment; third, the absence of a mind of ignorance and delusion; fourth, the absence of a mind of envy and jealousy; fifth, the absence of a mind of cruelty and oppression.
"If there were such a person, this illness would surely be cured.
The king said to his physicians,
"If such a person were to come to me, I alone would be free from this poison."
He immediately cut the flesh from his own body and gave it to him so that it might join with the decoction; the patient took it and was cured, whereupon he immediately set forth upon the Mahāyāna.
(7) Once there was a householder who constantly aspired to see Mañjuśrī.

The householder then made a great distribution of alms and prepared high seats. Upon their completion, there appeared an old man who was exceedingly ugly; mucus flowed from his eyes, snot from his nose, and saliva from his mouth. Seeing him, the householder thought as he sat upon the high seat:
"I have prepared these high seats today for the sake of noble śramaṇas who ought to sit upon them; what kind of person are you?"
He then dragged [the image] to the ground.
Having completed the offering, the householder lit lamps and burned incense within the Buddhist temple, saying:
"By means of this merit, may I behold Mañjuśrī in this present life."
He then returned home and lay down, utterly exhausted. In a dream, someone said to him:
"If you wish to see Mañjuśrī, you will not recognize him when you see him. The old man upon the high seat before you is precisely Mañjuśrī; you must pull him down to the ground."
"In this way, though we have seen him seven times in succession, we did not recognize him; how then could we see Mañjuśrī?
If one seeks the Bodhisattva path, one should maintain an equal mind toward all people.
When one who seeks the bodhisattva path encounters Mañjuśrī, he shall immediately go to test them and recognize this intention.
(8) A parable is told regarding the impermanence of the home.

There was a great tree whose fruits were like two-sheng jars. When the fruits were nearly ripe, a crow flew there and perched high upon a branch; as a fruit fell, it struck the crow's head and killed it.
Seeing this, the tree deity spoke in verse:
"The crow came seeking no death; The fruit fell, not for the sake of the crow.
The fruit ripened and the crow should die; It is the convergence of causes and conditions that makes it so."

"When a person is in the world, the convergence of their transgressions and blessings occurs according to its timing, whether slow or swift; there is no bypassing this sequence. A wise person feels no resentment when encountering transgression and feels no joy when receiving blessing. Only then does one become a true believer who accepts and upholds the Buddha’s words without departing from them."

Within the three realms, there are ninety-six kinds of paths; worldly people each revere their respective objects of devotion, hoping that the spirits will provide benefit. These various minor paths do not understand how to cultivate merit; how then could they uphold true virtue?

The reason for this is that they do not recognize the supreme brilliance of the Triple Gem, do not uphold the pure sincerity of the Five Precepts, and lack the profound insight of the Eightfold Path; how then could they provide protection and salvation to humanity?

For this reason, it is merely called "barren soil. (9) There are those who can revere the Triple Gem, observing that [the law] penetrates the three periods of time; they clearly understand the blessings of the heavenly realms and discern the punishments of Mount Tai. Reaching the height of faith in the Three Jewels, they block the path to the three miserable destinies; exerting the power of wisdom, they dispel the darkness of delusion within the three realms. Cultivating the pure divine water of the six perfections, they wash away the filth of the six afflictions. Thus, they are able to treat wealth lightly and sacrifice portions of their own bodies and speech, practicing impartial giving to establish the foundation for future lives.
A gift bestowed once brings a ten-thousandfold reward as swiftly as an echo responds to a sound; therefore it is said:
"The Great Way is the fertile field of the triple world.
How is this made clear?

In the past, when King Aśoka was a young child, he encountered the Buddha on the road; overcome with joy, he offered a small amount of sand with a sincere heart to the Buddha. By virtue of this merit, he became a holy king, ruling over sixteen great nations spanning four hundred thousand li.
To clarify this by means of an illustration: the Buddha is the most excellent field of merit. Formerly, the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was a person from the time of the past Buddha Vipaśyin.

By performing a single act of bathing for the assembly of monks, his merit spontaneously pursued him through successive births until he was born into the Śākya clan. His body was adorned with five or six of the marks of a great man, and his divine countenance shone with a golden luster. Riding upon the blessings of his previous lives, he appeared in the same world as the Buddha; by applying himself with refined diligence at the site of enlightenment, he immediately attained the six supernormal powers.
If those of antiquity bestowed even a single gift and yet received vast retribution, how much more so for you, donors, who are now able to practice extensively?
Through such universal conduct, you shall surely attain the Honorable Title; may your joy increase and you widely deliver all beings.
10 (Ten) Dharma Words: "The defiled spirit remains indestructible for billions of kalpas; it undergoes the torments of birth and death until the Way is attained.

Formerly, five hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king whose diligence and courage were rare in the world. For three months at one time, he made offerings to sixty thousand śramaṇas with sweet-smelling delicacies of the finest flavors in the world. Among them, the foremost elder was a man of the Path who had extensively mastered all scriptures, fathomed the past and understood the present, and had attained arhatship.

Four hundred and eighty *li* to the east of this country is a king who supports five hundred Brahmins with all the finest things of the world. He provides them with a hundred kinds of banners and streamers, adorned with silk, pure cotton, gold, jewels, and various other items; each banner is worth five hundred taels of gold, and he entertains them with such musical performances.
To whoever was capable of performing this craft, he would give it to them.

When the poor people of various kingdoms heard that the king of that country possessed such treasures, they gathered from all four directions like clouds, numbering five hundred men. Their route passed by the vihāra, and each practiced the craft with the intent of obtaining those treasures; however, their provisions being exhausted, they were unable to reach their destination, so they went before the Elder and requested to become śramaṇas.

The Elder then observed him and saw that he was formerly a servant in the household of a nobleman during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin; he had once prepared food and drink for practitioners and had heard the words of the Dharma. From that time until now, he has naturally received blessings among the devas and humans, and while his blessings have now come to an end, the influence of those words of the Dharma still remains. "These individuals are capable of being delivered," [the Elder thought].
He immediately shaved off his beard and hair and conferred upon him the precepts. As they were about to enter the palace for a meal, the king was filled with great joy.

The Master, perceiving his intention, explained to him that this food must not be consumed recklessly; if one eats this food without the utmost sincerity, one shall be reborn as an ox, a horse, or a slave for the king throughout successive kalpas.
When five hundred newly ordained bhikṣus heard this, they were struck with fear; they resolved their wills with vigor and diligence, and within ninety days, all attained arhatship.

Having realized the Path, the bhikṣus wished to recount their own experiences from beginning to end. They then ran out in haste, shouting as they entered the king’s gate to engage in a wrestling match: "I shall wrestle the three poisons, the twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates, and the six sense-fields! Who among you can face me?"
The assembly sat in stunned silence, wondering, "What words are these?

The bhikṣus replied, "We originally practiced the arts to obtain wealth and offerings; now, as śramaṇas, we have attained arhatship ourselves. We have already extinguished all the evils of the three realms, and by the grace of the Great Master, our happiness is boundless."

11. (11) Once upon a time, there lived two brothers who were of great power, wealth, and noble status, possessing immeasurable assets. When their parents passed away, they were left with no one to rely upon.
Although they were brothers, their aspirations and thoughts differed:
the elder brother delighted in the Way and its principles, while the younger brother cherished his family estate, official rank, and salary, coveting worldly glory and sensual pleasures.
They lived near the Pāṭaligāma Kukkuta Monastery, not far from it.

The elder brother devoted himself exclusively to study, seeking instruction in the Way of the Sutras, and did not involve himself in the family’s affairs. Seeing that his brother did not attend to domestic matters, the younger brother constantly harbored resentment toward him, saying:

"We are brothers, and our parents passed away early; we have struggled with great hardship to maintain our livelihood, yet you instead abandon the family business to pursue śramaṇas and listen to Buddhist scriptures."
"How could a śramaṇa possibly give you clothing, wealth, or treasures?

Your family will become increasingly impoverished and your resources will dwindle day by day; people will mock you, saying that you are indolent and negligent, and that your lineage will come to an end."
"Generally, one who is a son should establish merit and achievements, continuing the meritorious deeds of his parents without letting them fall into disuse; only then is he a filial son.

His elder brother replied to him, saying, "To transform one's parents through the Way—by means of the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, making offerings to the Triple Gem, practicing the six perfections, and sitting in meditation with mindfulness and concentration—is what constitutes filial piety."
The Way and the secular world are opposites, a natural law: that which the Way delights in is what the secular world detests; that which the secular world prizes is what the Way despises.
The wisdom of the intelligent and the folly of the ignorant do not align in counsel, just as light and darkness cannot coexist.
Therefore, the wise leave darkness for light to attain the reality of the Way.
What you now delight in is the "self" of suffering and affliction;
it is entirely empty, void, false, and unreal, yet through delusion you calculate it to exist—how could you know its bitterness?
The younger brother harbored resentment and remained headstrong and unfaithful. Seeing this, the elder brother said to him:
"You are greedy for household affairs and regard wealth as precious; I delight in the Way of the Sūtras and regard wisdom as a treasure."

Now, wishing to renounce the household life and take refuge in the field of merit, I reckon that this life entrusted to the world is as fleeting as a speck of dust blown by the wind; for when impermanence suddenly arrives, one will be ensnared by transgressions. Therefore, I renounce the world to avoid danger and seek safety.
When the younger brother saw that his elder brother’s will was directed toward the Way and its righteousness, he remained silent and offered no reply.

The elder brother then left home to become a śramaṇa; day and night he applied himself with diligence, reciting the sūtras and contemplating the Way. With single-mindedness he practiced seated meditation, discerning and reflecting without ever resting or succumbing to indolence. Thus he perfected the faculties, the powers, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; his practice accorded with the teachings of the sūtras and dharmas, and he attained the realization of the fruit of the Way.
He went to his younger brother’s place and exhorted him to follow the Dharma, saying:
“The five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are the foundation for rebirth in heaven; generosity and the pursuit of the Way are the basis for attaining wisdom.
Upon hearing these words, the younger brother’s anger flared even more, and he immediately replied to his elder brother:

"You ought to be expelled yourself; you have neglected your family duties and ruined our household. You may do as you please alone, but do not instruct me further. Leave my presence at once and do not involve yourself in my affairs."
The elder brother then departed.

The younger brother, however, was greedily preoccupied with his family estate without ceasing; he never established his mind in the Dharma, and upon the end of his life, he fell among cattle, becoming exceedingly fat and large.

A merchant purchased the salt and transported it for sale; after several round trips, the ox became emaciated and exhausted, unable to proceed further. As he struggled up the slope, he grew weary and collapsed, unable to rise; though the merchant lashed him with a whip, the ox only shook his head and moved with great difficulty.
At that time, the elder brother was traveling through the air, flying in the void. Seeing this from afar, he immediately reflected, "I know not from where he has come.
Upon examining his origin, he saw that it was originally his younger brother, and so he spoke to him, saying:

"Brother, where now is that house, field, and land which you so eagerly cherished? Why have you cast yourself down into the womb of an ox? He then used his supernormal power to illuminate and reveal his original destiny;

immediately recognizing it, tears fell from him as he reproached himself for his past unwholesome conduct—his stinginess, greed, and envy; his lack of faith in the Buddha-dharma and his contempt for the Noble Assembly; his indulgence in self-will and refusal to believe his elder brother’s words; and his defiance of the Holy Teachings through obstinacy and self-opinionatedness. "Because of this, I have fallen among the oxen. Now that I am exhausted, weary, and debilitated, what can be done to reach repentance?"
The elder brother, knowing his younger brother’s thoughts, was moved with deep sorrow and compassion. He immediately explained the full circumstances of the matter to the owner of the ox, saying:

"This was originally my younger brother. Lacking faith in the Triple Gem, he turned away from the truth toward falsehood; being stingy, envious, self-indulgent, and greedily seeking without giving, he has fallen among the oxen. Emaciated, weak, and miserable, he is truly pitiable. Now that he is extremely old and exhausted, he is no longer fit for work; I pray you grant him to me to sustain his remaining life."

Upon hearing this, the merchant immediately gave it as an offering; he then took the ox back to the monastery, where he had it recite the names of the Triple Gem and provide it with food at the appropriate times. When its life came to an end, it was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the various merchants each thought to themselves:

"We have diligently pursued our livelihoods without weariness, yet we were unable to practice giving, nor did we honor the Dharma, nor understand the principles of the Way; even in death, we fear we shall not escape this same fate."

They then departed together from their home, abandoning their wives and children and casting away all their precious possessions. They became śramaṇas, practicing with diligence and without slackening, and they all attained the Way.

Viewed from this perspective, worldly wealth and treasures do not benefit a person; rather, by revering the Triple Gem, cultivating the self, and studying wisdom, and by hearing extensively and practicing the Path, one attains peace life after life.

12. Once, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a poor household that had a grapevine in its courtyard with several clusters of fruit upon it; they thought of immediately offering it to a practitioner.
At that time, the king had previously invited him for a month’s meal; however, the poor family’s resources were insufficient.
The king had formally granted him a month's leave, so he obtained a practitioner of the Way and offered him as a gift, saying to the practitioner:
"I have intended to offer you for a month, and now my wish has been fulfilled."
The practitioner said to the upāsikā,
"I have accepted your offering for one month.
The upāsikā replied:
"I have merely offered a single cluster of grapes; how can this constitute a month's offering?
The practitioner said, "If you simply maintain the intention to give for one month, that itself constitutes a month."
"There are eighteen things that are extremely difficult for people in this world:
first, the difficulty of encountering a Buddha in the world;
second, even if one encounters a Buddha, the difficulty of succeeding in becoming a human being."
Third, even if one succeeds in becoming a human being, it is difficult to be born in the central lands;
fourth, even if one is born in the central lands, it is difficult to be born into a noble lineage;
fifth, even if one is born into a noble lineage, it is difficult for the four limbs and six sense organs to be fully intact.
Sixth, even if one possesses the four limbs and six sense organs in their entirety, wealth is difficult to obtain;
seventh, even if one obtains wealth, a virtuous friend is difficult to find;
eighth, even if one finds a virtuous friend, wisdom is difficult to attain.
Ninth, even if one possesses wisdom, it is difficult to have a virtuous mind;
tenth, even if one possesses a virtuous mind, it is difficult to be able to practice giving;
eleventh, even if one is able to practice giving, it is difficult to encounter a person who is noble, good, and virtuous.
Twelfth, even if one encounters a person who is wise, virtuous, and endowed with merit, it is difficult to approach them;
thirteenth, even if one has approached them, it is difficult to find a suitable opportunity;
fourteenth, even if one finds a suitable opportunity, it is difficult to have one’s inquiries heard and to speak of what is correct and upright.
Sixteenth, even if one attains right centrality, one must resolve the difficulties regarding wisdom;
seventeenth, even if one attains the resolution of wisdom, one must be able to receive the various difficulties of the profound sutras—
these constitute the eighteen matters.
Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables (Za piyu jing)
